lesson.title: The Sixteenth Amendment: How the Income Tax Became Constitutional
lesson.summary: Ratified in February 1913, the Sixteenth Amendment gave Congress the power to levy an income tax without apportioning it among the states by population, overturning an 1895 Supreme Court decision and giving the federal government a new, more flexible and more progressive source of revenue.
lesson.body:
For most of the nineteenth century, the federal government funded itself mainly through tariffs on imported goods and excise taxes, revenue sources that fell disproportionately on consumers and working people, since tariffs raised the price of everyday goods regardless of a buyer's income. Critics, going back to the Populist movement's 1892 Omaha Platform, had argued for a graduated income tax as a fairer alternative, one that would ask more from the wealthy and less from ordinary households. Congress actually passed a modest income tax in 1894, but the Supreme Court struck it down the following year in Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co., ruling that an income tax on income derived from property counted as a direct tax under the Constitution and therefore had to be apportioned among the states according to population, a requirement that made any meaningful income tax practically impossible to design.

The Pollock decision effectively closed off the income tax as a policy option for nearly two decades, but the underlying argument for it did not go away. Progressive Era reformers picked up the cause that populists had raised earlier, contending that a modern industrial economy needed a tax system that could reach the vast fortunes being accumulated by figures like the industrial and financial titans whose companies muckrakers such as Ida Tarbell had spent years investigating, rather than relying so heavily on tariffs that burdened working families disproportionately. This connected the income tax fight directly to the era's broader argument, inherited from debates over federalism, about how much power the federal government should hold relative to the states and relative to concentrated private wealth.

Momentum built steadily through the early 1900s, and Congress passed the amendment in 1909 with support from figures across the political spectrum, including President Taft, who saw it partly as a way to defuse pressure for even more aggressive tax proposals. The necessary three-quarters of state legislatures ratified it by February 1913, just weeks before Woodrow Wilson took office, and the Sixteenth Amendment specifically authorized Congress to tax incomes from whatever source derived without apportionment among the states, directly overriding the Pollock precedent.

The amendment's practical effect grew slowly at first, since the original 1913 income tax applied only to a small share of the wealthiest Americans, but it created the constitutional foundation for what would eventually become the federal government's primary source of revenue. In doing so, it marked one of the clearest victories of the Progressive Era's broader project: using federal power, expanded through formal constitutional change rather than mere legislation, to reshape the economic relationship between government, the wealthy, and ordinary citizens.
